newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac fails to quash election, reshuffle talk.
newsitem.headline: Chirac fails to quash election, reshuffle talk.

text.p: Despite denials, President Jacques Chirac failed to calm rumours in France on Thursday about a snap election or cabinet reshuffle, and the opposition Socialist party said it was ready to contest a vote.

Amid political shadow-boxing, the Socialists accused Chirac of mulling parliamentary elections a year early to renew the centre-right majority before a new bout of austerity to help France qualify for a single European currency.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure denied speculation that Chirac might justify an election by arguing that greater fiscal rigour was needed. "We have no budgetary problems at the moment," he said.

An early election "is not impossible", said Pierre Mazeaud, a leading parliamentarian in the Gaullist party founded by Chirac. "It is part of the solutions that seem to be under consideration at the moment."

"One may consider it necessary to get a second wind," he told France Inter radio. Economic growth has picked up slightly, as has the popularity of Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe in opinion polls this year.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, accusing Chirac of lacking confidence in Juppe's policies, said his party was ready for any dissolution of the National Assembly, whose five-year term runs out in March 1998.
"If there are any decisions to be taken, let him (Chirac) take them," Jospin said during a visit to Vierzon, central France.
Chirac might be tempted to call an election to secure a renewed majority in parliament for the rest of his seven-year term.

It might also allow him to seize the initiative on European integration and ensure that campaigning does not coincide with European Union debate early next year on which countries make the grade for a single currency from 1999.
A cabinet reshuffle offers a less dramatic alternative that might help heal rifts in the fractious ruling coalition.

Chirac has so far failed to quash the speculation. An official source at his office said on Wednesday that rumours of a reshuffle or early election were baseless but added: "The president has time on his hands for reflection."

"Shhh. The president is reflecting", the left-leaning daily Liberation said in a front-page headline. The conservative daily Le Figaro went so far as to say that any dissolution of parliament would probably mean a two-stage vote on June 1 and 8.
The daily Le Monde said some of Chirac's closest allies reckoned early elections improbable, even though it said Juppe was in favour.
"Can Mr Chirac take a personal risk to let the prime minister gamble on legislative elections in which (Juppe) would be the main victor?" it asked.

If Chirac did call a snap election, it would be the first time in France's 39-year-old Fifth Republic that a president has dissolved the Assembly without a major crisis brewing. The ruling coalition controls 80 percent of the Assembly's seats.
A reshuffle would be more mundane -- Juppe's two-year-old government has had one reshuffle already, in November 1995.

In the National Assembly, speaker Philippe Seguin ruled out breaking off a debate about poverty on Thursday to discuss proposals about campaign financing. "The Assembly must impassively continue to respect its agenda," he said.
